nameStory: Deertongue gets its memorable name from the shape and texture of its leaves, which are long, narrow, and lance-shaped like a deer's tongue. The resemblance is especially striking when you run your fingers along the smooth to slightly hairy leaf surface, which feels remarkably similar to touching a deer's actual tongue!
description: Deertongue is a clump-forming perennial grass that can grow quite tall, reaching up to 4.5 feet in height. It spreads by underground stems called rhizomes, creating patches of hairy stems topped with narrow, lance-shaped leaves. This native New England grass has an interesting double flowering strategy - it produces both visible, open flower clusters and hidden flowers tucked away in leaf sheaths that never open at all. It's a hardy grass that thrives in poor soils where other plants struggle.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lance-shaped leaves up to 10 inches long and about an inch wide, arranged alternately up the stem with 5-10 leaves per stem. Feel smooth to slightly hairy and can be somewhat rigid to the touch.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Two types of flowers: open, airy panicles (branched flower clusters) visible at stem tops in early summer, plus hidden cleistogamous flowers tucked inside leaf sheaths that appear later and never open.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms clumps from underground rhizomes, with multiple hairy stems rising 2-4.5 feet tall. Stems feel distinctly fuzzy when you run your hand along them.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny seeds produced in enormous quantities - about 400,000 per pound! Seeds are small and numerous, readily shaken from mature seed heads with a gentle touch.

habitat: Deertongue thrives in acidic, nutrient-poor soils that challenge many other plants, making it common in disturbed areas, old fields, and forest edges throughout New England. It's particularly fond of sandy or thin soils and can even tolerate soils with high aluminum content. You'll often find it growing alongside other hardy grasses and wildflowers in areas recovering from disturbance.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from rhizomes, and stems begin their upward growth with fresh green leaves unfurling alternately up the fuzzy stems.
seasonality.summer: Open panicle flowers appear at stem tops in early summer, creating airy, branched seed heads. Later in summer, the hidden cleistogamous flowers develop inside leaf sheaths.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and can be easily shaken from the dried seed heads. Foliage begins to turn brown and stems become more brittle to the touch.
seasonality.winter: Dried stems and seed heads persist, providing food for birds. Dead stems feel papery and break easily when handled.

funFact: Deertongue is essentially a grass that hedges its bets - it produces secret flowers hidden in its leaf sheaths that never open and fertilize themselves, ensuring reproduction even when weather or pollinators fail the visible flowers!
confusionNotes: Deertongue can be confused with other Dichanthelium grasses, but its combination of lance-shaped leaves, hairy stems, and dual flowering strategy helps distinguish it. Look for those hidden flowers tucked in the leaf sheaths later in the season - that's your smoking gun for deertongue identification.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'deertongue,' this grass isn't particularly favored by deer or livestock because it's low in nutrients. The name is purely about the leaf shape and texture, not its palatability to animals.
compareHints: Among the many Dichanthelium species in New England, deertongue stands out for its relatively large size (up to 4.5 feet), distinctly hairy stems, and lance-shaped leaves that can feel somewhat rigid. While species like starved witchgrass and forked witchgrass tend to be smaller and more delicate, deertongue forms substantial clumps with robust, fuzzy stems that you can easily feel when you brush against them.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Starved witchgrass is much more delicate and sparse than its relatives like deertongue or broad-leaved panic grass, which have wider leaves and more robust growth.
Among its many witchgrass relatives, forked witchgrass stands out for its distinctly Y-shaped branching pattern.
Among its Dichanthelium relatives, broad-leaved panic grass stands out for having the widest leaves - most other rosette grasses have much narrower, linear blades.

Among its rosette grass relatives, round-fruited rosette-panicgrass is distinguished primarily by its perfectly spherical seeds - most others like hairy rosette-panicgrass or deertongue have oval or egg-shaped seeds.
Among its many rosette grass relatives, hairy rosette-panicgrass stands out for its consistently fuzzy, velvety texture - most others like deertongue feel smooth or slightly rough.
Among its witchgrass relatives, Bosc's witchgrass tends to have broader leaves than Starved Witchgrass or Slim-leaf Witchgrass, but narrower leaves than broad-leaved panic grass.
Among its many rosette grass relatives, Slim-leaf Witchgrass stands out for having the narrowest leaves - most other Dichanthelium species have broader, more oval-shaped leaves.
Among its many Dichanthelium relatives in New England, variable witchgrass tends to be more adaptable to different moisture levels than most.
Among its witchgrass relatives, Small-fruited Witchgrass is distinguished primarily by its exceptionally tiny seeds - much smaller than deertongue or broad-leaved panic grass.
Wright's Rosette Grass differs from its relatives like deertongue and the various witchgrasses by forming more perfectly circular, compact rosettes rather than loose clumps.
Compared to its Dichanthelium relatives, slender panic grass is notably more delicate and fine-textured than broad-leaved panic grass, and lacks the dense hairiness of hairy rosette-panicgrass.
Northern witchgrass is distinguished from its Dichanthelium relatives primarily by its northern range preference and smaller overall size.

Among the many panic grass relatives in New England, velvet panicum stands out for its exceptionally soft, velvety texture - most other Dichanthelium species are hairy but not nearly as plush-feeling.
Unlike the more common deertongue with its broad leaves and dense shade tolerance, false bearded panic grass has much narrower leaves and prefers wet, open areas.

Among its many Dichanthelium relatives in New England, Heller's rosette grass stands out for its strong preference for partial shade rather than full sun, and its consistently neat rosette growth pattern.

Among the rosette grasses, Scribner's Panicgrass is distinguished by its relatively narrow rosette leaves compared to broad-leaved panic grass, and its more pointed leaf tips compared to the rounded leaves of deertongue.

Eaton's Witchgrass is distinguished from its many Dichanthelium relatives by subtle differences in leaf width, flower cluster branching patterns, and seed size - characteristics that often require expert identification.

Old-field panic grass differs from its many Dichanthelium relatives primarily by habitat preference - while species like deertongue prefer shady woodlands, old-field panic grass seeks out sunny, disturbed areas.
Among its many Dichanthelium relatives, old field panic grass is distinguished by its preference for truly open, disturbed habitats rather than woodland edges.
Among New England's rosette grasses, Lindheimer's panicgrass stands out for its nearly hairless leaves and preference for wetter soils.
Hemlock panic grass differs from its Dichanthelium relatives by its preference for coniferous rather than deciduous woods and its particularly delicate, narrow leaves.
